Context: In this poem, the author imagines what Sisyphus might have said if he could explain his actions and his understanding of the Greek mythological afterlife.
Title: Passage 3: Sisyphus’s Confession
Content: I’ll admit, the `text(first)` few times were agony (pure anguish).
I could barely move that rock and felt my hope near-extinguish.
Slow step by step, I heaved my burden and tried to set my will.
Drip, drap, drop, the gods cackled as I sweated on that hill.
I let them laugh, even stumbled a bit to encourage them to jest.
I made a great show of huffing and heaving and all the rest.
They bought it, of course, thanks to their hubris.
They assume I suffer — that no mortal would choose this.
Why do you think I wanted to outwit death —
that I cared if I took another breath?
Here, my lungs toil tirelessly, my limbs are lead,
but what an alternative to being dead!
In body and in flesh, no man can truly live forever.
But let the world know my deeds, or simply that I was clever.
Whether here or there, all will know the name
of Sisyphus, who nearly beat the gods at their own game.
Who — no, what would I be had I accepted my lot?
A dark shadow, incapable of even a `text(single)` thought.
Give me the struggle, then the satisfaction,
Even resentment is better than facing oblivion.
Now I set my hardened, calloused shoulder
into the familiar dips and valleys of my boulder.
I feel a smirk threaten to spread across my face.
Finally, the kind of storied destiny I can truly embrace.
But this quiet kind of contentment, I dare not let show.
What would the gods do next, should they know?
